q: The elements with low electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of anions. (2024)
e: Elements with high electron affinity easily gain electrons to form anions.

q: London dispersion forces are the strongest intermolecular forces. (2024)
e: London dispersion forces are the weakest intermolecular forces.

q: Many inorganic substances and millions of organic compounds have covalent bonding. (2024)
e: Covalent bonding is widespread in many inorganic compounds and almost all organic compounds.

q: Hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole interaction that occurs between nonpolar molecules. (2025)
e: Hydrogen bonding occurs between polar molecules containing hydrogen bonded to highly electronegative atoms (N, O, F).

q: Two electrons with the same spin can occupy the same orbital. (2024)
e: According to Pauli's exclusion principle, two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins.

q: Silicon (III) oxide is an example of a giant covalent molecule. (2024)
e: Silicon(IV) oxide (SiO2) is an example of a giant covalent structure.

q: The higher the value of electronegativity, the smaller is the atom's attraction to electrons. (2024)
e: The higher the electronegativity, the greater the atom's attraction for electrons.

q: The total dipole moment of CO2 is not zero and it is a non-polar molecule. (2024)
e: CO2 is a linear molecule whose individual bond dipoles cancel out, making its total dipole moment zero.

q: Ionic bonding generally occurs between reactive metals and reactive non-metals. (2025)
e: Reactive metals easily lose electrons and reactive non-metals easily gain electrons to form ionic bonds.

q: The octet rule does not apply to d-block elements. (2025)
e: Transition elements (d-block) involve d-orbitals in bonding and frequently do not follow the octet rule.

q: In water molecules, hydrogens are partially positive and oxygens are partially negative. (2024)
e: Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, pulling shared electron density toward itself.

q: There is no intermolecular hydrogen bonding between ether molecules. (2024)
e: Ethers lack hydrogen atoms directly attached to oxygen, so they cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other.

q: The ionic compounds are always neutral. (2025)
e: The total positive charges of the cations balance out the total negative charges of the anions.

q: The hydrogen bond is weaker than all other intermolecular forces. (2025)
e: Hydrogen bonds are significantly stronger than ordinary dipole-dipole interactions and London dispersion forces.

q: Aufbau principle states that electrons are filled in the higher energy atomic orbitals before filling lower energy ones. (2024)
e: The Aufbau principle states that electrons fill lower energy atomic orbitals before higher energy ones.

q: Any non-polar covalent bond has a zero dipole moment. (2024)
e: Non-polar covalent bonds share electrons equally, resulting in zero dipole moment.

q: The molecular shape of the ammonia molecule, NH3, is tetrahedral. (2025)
e: The molecular shape of NH3 is trigonal pyramidal due to one lone pair on the nitrogen atom.

q: Na+ and Cl- ions, have the electronic configuration of the noble gas Ne. (2025)
e: Na+ has the electronic configuration of Ne, whereas Cl- has the configuration of Ar.

q: Polar covalent bond is formed between two similar non-metal atoms. (2025)
e: Polar covalent bonds are formed between different non-metal atoms with different electronegativities.

q: The cubic unit cell can have two types. (2025)
e: There are three types of cubic unit cells: simple cubic, body-centred cubic, and face-centred cubic.

q: A double bond is formed by sharing only one pair of electrons between two atoms. (2025)
e: A double bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons between two atoms.

q: In ionic compounds, the cations and anions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction. (2025)
e: Oppositively charged ions attract each other through strong electrostatic forces.

q: The hydrogen bond is the weakest of all intermolecular forces. (2024)
e: Hydrogen bonds are the strongest class of intermolecular forces.

q: Any non-polar covalent bond has a zero dipole moment. (2024)
e: In a non-polar covalent bond, electron distribution is symmetrical, giving a dipole moment of zero.

q: Carbon dioxide is a non-polar molecule and the dipole moment is not zero. (2024)
e: Carbon dioxide is non-polar because its symmetrical linear structure causes its dipole moment to be zero.

q: Face-centred cubic unit cell is a cubic cell with an atom on each corner, and another in the centre of the cube. (2024)
e: A face-centred cubic unit cell has an atom at each corner and one at the centre of each face.

q: The higher the value of the electronegativity, the greater is the atom's attraction to electrons. (2025)
e: Electronegativity measures the ability of an atom to attract bonding electrons.

q: Lewis structure of carbon monoxide molecule consists of two covalent bond and one coordinate bond. (2025)
e: The CO molecule contains a triple bond composed of two standard covalent bonds and one dative coordinate bond.

q: London dispersion forces are the strongest intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances. (2025)
e: London dispersion forces are the weakest intermolecular forces, although they exist in all molecular substances.

q: In a metallic bond, the valence electrons of the atoms are very loosely held, forming a common electron cloud. (2025)
e: Metallic bonds consist of positive metal ions surrounded by a delocalized cloud of valence electrons.

q: The formation of H3O+ ion is an example of the formation of a dative bond. (2025)
e: In H3O+, oxygen donates a lone pair of electrons to a hydrogen ion (H+) to form a dative bond.

q: The boiling points of some metals become lower compared with the ionic compounds. (2025)
e: Metals with weaker metallic bonding have lower boiling points than standard ionic lattice structures.

q: The octet rule does not apply to s-block elements. (2025)
e: The octet rule generally applies to main group s-block elements.

q: Unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice that shows the three dimensional pattern of the entire crystal. (2025)
e: The unit cell is the fundamental structural unit that reproduces the entire crystal lattice in three dimensions.

q: For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its period number in the Periodic Table. (2026)
e: The number of valence electrons is determined by the main group number, whereas the period number indicates the principal energy level.

q: The electronegativity of bonded atoms and the geometry of molecules play an important role in determining their polarity. (2026)
e: Molecular polarity depends on individual bond polarities and the overall symmetry of the molecular geometry.

q: Only valence electrons can take part in chemical bonding. (2026)
e: Inner shell electrons are shielded and held tightly by the nucleus, so only valence electrons participate in bonding.
